title: KFC Japan creates contract with Dr. Doom for Marvel supervillainy fried chicken
description: If doom is coming, you may as well treat yourself to some fried chicken first. Usually when there’s an eye-catching collaboration coming up, it’s between two parties who are widely loved. You know, Studio Ghibli and Uniqlo, Pokémon and manga artist Tetsuo Hara, Hello Kitty and soft, pillowy toilet paper, those sorts of combinations. But […]
content:
If doom is coming, you may as well treat yourself to some fried chicken first.

Usually when there’s an eye-catching collaboration coming up, it’s between two parties who are widely loved. You know, Studio Ghibli and Uniqlo, Pokémon and manga artist Tetsuo Hara, Hello Kitty and soft, pillowy toilet paper, those sorts of combinations.

But while KFC Japan is an organization most people have no problem with, support is much less universal for their latest creative partner: Doctor Doom.

【重要なお知らせ】

この度KFCは、ドゥームズデイ対策の一環として、マーベル最新のヴィラン、ドクター・ドゥーム氏との契約締結を完了いたしましたので、ここにお知らせいたします。… pic.twitter.com/mAmL9mp2qf

— ケンタッキーフライドチキン (@KFC_jp) November 16, 2026

“KFC has entered into a contract with Dr. Doom” says KFC Japan in announcing their joint venture with the Marvel Comics supervillain. “KFC is devoted to upholding its side of the contract by continuing to fry up delicious chicken and offer it with friendly customer service even as Doomsday approaches.”

The doctor and the colonel are working together in the runup to the theatrical premiere of Avengers: Doomsday, the long-awaited next chapter in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s most popular franchise. Starting November 25, KFC Japan will be serving the Double Doom Burger.

This new version of the chain’s Double Down “sandwich” continues its tradition of replacing the bread with boneless Original Recipe chicken cutlets. Those cutlets are wrapped around a hash brown patty with slices of cheese on either side, and the Double Doom adds in a Dr. Doom-like green Smokey Green Mayo made with garlic, honey, and lime, plus some sinister-sounding “Doom Cola Sauce.” Bundled with fries and a drink, the 1,750-yen (US$11) Double Doom Burger Set will be available in limited quantities at 56 KFC Japan branches.

▼ The full list of branches can be found here, with the ones Tokyo travelers are most likely to find themselves near being KFC Japan’s Ikebukuro Nishiguchi, Ginza INZ, and Shinjuku Toho Building locations.

Meanwhile, from November 25 all KFC Japan branches will be offering the Doom Bucket (called the “Doom Barrel” in Japanese).

This is, thankfully, not a bucket of misfortune, but a bucket of chicken containing two pieces of Original Recipe and a Colonel’s Crispy boneless chicken tender. The crossover condiments here are Smokey Green Mayo dipping sauce and a packet of Lime and Smoked Chili Doom Seasoning powder, and once again you get fries on the side, as part of the 1,650-yen set.

Diners buying either of the Dr. Doom-themed items will receive a Doomsday sticker with a QR code on the back, which they can use to be entered for a chance to win one of four prizes, either a KFC/Dr. Doom jacket, sweatshirt, cap, or one of five figures of KFC founder Colonel Sanders cosplaying as characters who appear in the movie.

▼ Colonel Sanders Gambit makes sense, since they share Southern roots.

Though both menu items are officially scheduled for sale between November 25 and December 17, they’re also both listed as limited-quantity, so availability might not stretch all the way to the end of that period. For those who don’t want to miss this chance to dine like Doom, the Double Doom Burger Set and Doom Barrel can be reserved through KFC Japan’s website or mobile app starting November 20 at 6 a.m.

title: Tommy Lee Jones becomes Pikachu in Japan for Suntory
description: Alien Jones turns his attention to Pokémon. Among Hollywood celebrities, Tommy Lee Jones has always had an old-fashioned, no-nonsense persona. His aura of down-to-earth unpretentiousness makes him the kind of guy who could, conceivably, reach for Suntory’s Boss canned coffee when he’s craving caffeinated refreshment, as the brand is known for being good-tasting without needing […]
content:
Alien Jones turns his attention to Pokémon.

Among Hollywood celebrities, Tommy Lee Jones has always had an old-fashioned, no-nonsense persona. His aura of down-to-earth unpretentiousness makes him the kind of guy who could, conceivably, reach for Suntory’s Boss canned coffee when he’s craving caffeinated refreshment, as the brand is known for being good-tasting without needing to resort to outlandish special flavors.

Of course, that atmosphere of solemn dignity is slightly diluted in Jones’ latest ads for Boss, in which the 80-year-old veteran actor dresses as Pikachu.

The unexpected outfit comes as part of Boss’ collaboration with the 30th anniversary celebration of the Pokémon franchise. Jones has been a regular pitchman for Boss for many years, one of the few Hollywood celebrities to stick around with a regular marketing deal in Japan after many of his brethren started avoiding such work, as Internet video-sharing platforms mean such silly side projects can no longer be limited to viewers in Japan only like they were in the 1980s and ‘90s. Not only is Jones unconcerned about being laughed at, that’s arguably the entire point of his ads for Boss, in which he portrays “Alien Jones,” a stern-faced extraterrestrial who comes to earth to observe hard-working humans in their natural environments.

Suntory is currently running a promotion in which customers who buy a six-pack of Boss coffee between now and January 31 have a chance of winning a jacket with the Boss logo and the Pokémon 30th anniversary emblem. So to get into the spirit, Alien Jones is doing a little light Pikachu cosplay. He’s also apparently expanded his observational operations to include Pokémon species, such as in this short video where he learns about Psyduck.

The Pokémon called Psyduck.

Similarly to the people living on this planet, when it feels excessive stress it develops an escalating headache, and cradles its head in response. There is a sense of satisfaction in seeing it overwhelm its surroundings with its strong psychic powers.

With Suntory being one of Japan’s biggest beverage makers, we’ll probably be seeing the Pikachu Tommy Lee Jones popping up on posters and signboards at various stores in Japan, but if you want to be sure of spotting him, Suntory will be taking over the Ueno Canvas and adjacent concourse outside the Chuo Gate of Ueno Station in Tokyo from now until November 22 so that their Poké-fied alien can greet travelers in large-scale style.

title: What is Japan’s Yamagata soba, and do you have to go to Yamagata to eat it?
description: Our traveling reporter has his first experience with Yamagata’s style of buckwheat noodles, but he could have eaten them much closer to home too. Fans of Japanese noodles are no doubt already aware of the regional ramen differences, such as Hokkaido’s heavy concentration of restaurants that specialize in miso broth and Fukuoka’s preference for tonkotsu […]
content:
Our traveling reporter has his first experience with Yamagata’s style of buckwheat noodles, but he could have eaten them much closer to home too.

Fans of Japanese noodles are no doubt already aware of the regional ramen differences, such as Hokkaido’s heavy concentration of restaurants that specialize in miso broth and Fukuoka’s preference for tonkotsu (pork stock). Different parts of Japan sometimes also do their soba/buckwheat noodles differently too, and on a recent trip to Japan’s northeastern Tohoku region our Japanese-language reporter P.K. Sanjun got to try Yamagata soba for the first time.

First, a little introduction to the characteristics of Yamagata soba. While all soba noodles contain buckwheat flour, in Yamagata they use unpolished buckwheat flour, which leaves little pieces of the grain’s husk in the dough. The result is soba noodles with a darker color and more pronounced buckwheat scent, plus a coarser texture and extra-chewy consistency. Zooming in closer still, we come to the representative types of soba for different parts of Yamagata Prefecture, with the one we’re tasting today being a specific style of niku soba (“meat soba”) that originated in the town of Kahoku.

In most parts of Japan, the meat that you’ll find in niku soba is strips of either pork or beef. Kahoku’s niku soba, though, uses chicken, both in strips and in thicker chashu-style cuts. The broth is made with chicken stock too, and while some connoisseurs say Yamagata niku soba is a dish/bowl best served cold, you can order it hot too, which is what Sanun did on his visit to Yamagata soba specialty restaurant Toshichi.

This restaurant is actually in the city of Sendai, which is in Miyagi Prefecture, Yamagata’s neighbor to the east, but thus still within the Yamagata soba sphere of influence. The restaurant, a 15-minute walk from Sendai Station, is only open for three hours each day, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., but there was a long line of local businessmen waiting to get in when P.K. arrived (the above photo was snapped after his meal), so he had high hopes that a very good meal was awaiting him.

Prices for niku soba start at 760 yen (US$4.80), but P.K. splurged for a large-size bowl for 880 yen, and he also tacked on a topping order of tempura squid tentacles, a popular accompaniment for soba in Yamagata.

After a short wait, a very hearty-looking bowl of noodles was placed before P.K., with a small pile of sliced green onion at its center.

He started with a sip of the broth, which had a faint gold hue to it from the chicken stock and a meaty sweetness as it splashed onto his taste buds.

The noodles were thick and dark, with a speckled pattern from the bits of soba husk. They were, as promised, extremely chewy, and if they hadn’t been softened up from soaking in the hot broth, P.K. thinks his jaw would have been tired out from trying to bite through them. They were tasty, though, and very filling. P.K. has a pretty big appetite on most days, but even he had no complaints about the quantity of noodles.

There’s more firmness to be found in the chicken, too. As is often the style with Yamagata soba, Toshichi uses mature chickens for its meat and broth, and while the meat isn’t tough, stringy, or otherwise low-quality, it does require some chewing. That just gives you more time to enjoy the flavor, though. And last, the tempura squid was excellent as well, giving P.K. no regrets whatsoever about asking for the extra topping.

Again, this was P.K.’s first experience with Yamagata soba, and what he had specifically was one type of Yamagata soba, Kahoku-style niku soba, but he came away very impressed with how substantial-feeling and satisfying the noodles were. Lucky for him, it turns out in addition to its two Sendai locations, Toshichi also has a third branch in downtown Tokyo’s Hanzomon neighborhood, so he, or you, can enjoy a taste of Yamagata soba even if a trip up to Tohoku isn’t in your travel plans.

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new Christmas Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino
description: Serving up the tastiest Christmas tree, with layers of powdered green tea. At this time of year in Japan, you’ll start to see Christmas trees popping up all over the place, with their green hues brightening the landscape as the days get colder and shorter. It’s not the only place you’ll be seeing green, as […]
content:
Serving up the tastiest Christmas tree, with layers of powdered green tea.

At this time of year in Japan, you’ll start to see Christmas trees popping up all over the place, with their green hues brightening the landscape as the days get colder and shorter.

It’s not the only place you’ll be seeing green, as Starbucks Japan has just announced it will be welcoming the holiday season with a luxurious new Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino. Taking its inspiration from the famous Italian dessert, the new Frappuccino combines rich, creamy mascarpone with the bittersweet taste of matcha, creating a layered drink with generous amounts of Japanese tea flavour.

At the bottom of the cup, you’ll find a rich, concentrated matcha sauce filled with the delicious bittersweet umami notes of powdered green tea. In the middle is a Frappuccino base with an original blend of matcha powder, which, when combined with the bottom layer, is said to create a blend so tasty it’ll make matcha lovers swoon.

Topped with a generous layer of mascarpone cream, to recreate the creamy layer of a traditional tiramisu, the drink is sprinkled with a light dusting of matcha powder to finish.

According to Starbucks, the new Frappuccino was born from the desire to give the chain’s much-loved matcha a more festive feel, and tiramisu, with its distinctive layers of mascarpone cream, was deemed to be the perfect match for creating a special holiday drink.

It certainly looks like a delicious pairing for the holiday season, and it’ll be on the menu for a limited time from 20 November, priced from 707 yen (US$4.71).

title: We try Japan’s craziest energy drink…from a Street Fighter card!
description: This new product might look like a trading card, but it’s actually an energy drink.  Energy drinks usually come in bottles or cans, but right now in Japan there’s a new invention that’s blowing people’s minds. It’s a drink in a card, and at first glance, it looks exactly like an ordinary trading card, complete […]
content:
This new product might look like a trading card, but it’s actually an energy drink. 

Energy drinks usually come in bottles or cans, but right now in Japan there’s a new invention that’s blowing people’s minds. It’s a drink in a card, and at first glance, it looks exactly like an ordinary trading card, complete with Street Fighter characters, but they’re actually designed for you to put your lips on, so you can take a sip and get an energy hit, just like a character replenishing their HP.

Created by UHA Mikakuto, this unusual product goes by the official name ENERGY ARTS, and it was recently ranked fifth in Nikkei Trendy’s Top 30 Hit Predictions for 2027. At the moment, it’s such a rare product that it can only be purchased online, and as we were curious to find out how it works, our reporter Yayoi Saginomiya ordered a box from Amazon to test it out in person.

When her package arrived, Yayoi was surprised at how compact it was, with the box, containing 10 individual cards, being just a little bigger than the palm of her hand.

As a collaboration product with the popular fighting game Street Fighter 6, each individual packet features a selection from 24 exclusive designs: 23 different characters plus one group illustration. The designs are included at random, so Yayoi opened her 10 packets to see what she got, and she was happy to find that the only duplicate in her pack was the group illustration.

Now it was time to give it a try, and since her son was at home when the package arrived, she decided to let him try one to get his verdict as well. All you have to do to drink this card is hold it vertically with the plain white side (the side without the design) facing you, then bring it up to your mouth. Fold it with one hand, and…

▼ …take a sip!

Both Yayoi and her son couldn’t quite believe it when a little squirt of liquid released itself from the card straight into their mouths. It was easy to suck up, and although it might take a little practice the first few times, if you look closely at the white side, you’ll see a cross-shaped slit that shows you exactly where to fold it.

Each packet contains just 12 millilitres (0.4 ounces) of liquid, and according to the manufacturer, one of its major selling points is the fact that you can drink it in just 0.5 seconds. It’s convenient when you’re busy, and there’s no need to worry about leaving any unfinished drink behind.

However, after trying it in person, Yayoi found there was one issue she couldn’t overlook: the taste. If she’s being honest, it didn’t taste particularly good – it had a highly concentrated energy drink flavour, with a slightly medicinal aftertaste. That said, it’s certainly not undrinkable, so for a lot of people, and gamers in particular, it won’t be a dealbreaker. Yayoi’s son actually liked it and enthusiastically declared it delicious, so the taste is ultimately a matter of personal preference.

▼ Either way, it’s incredibly thin and compact, making it easy to slip into a suit pocket, which is what Yayoi’s husband chose to do.


▼ Or you can tuck it away inside a bag or pouch for times when you need an instant boost.

The Street Fighter designs make these a must-have for fans of the franchise, and although Yayoi isn’t particularly familiar with the series or its characters, even she got a kick out of the cards.

While the cards are currently only available online, through sites like the official UHA Mikakuto online store, Amazon and Rakuten, Yayoi reckons their popularity might just lead to a wider release in future.

Yayoi bought her box on Amazon for 3,383 yen (US$22), which works out to almost 340 yen per packet. While that might be a dealbreaker for some people, as it’s pretty pricey for a 12-millilitre energy drink, for gamers and fans of the franchise, the chance to drink from a Street Fighter card is a priceless experience.

title: SmaGO “smart trash cans” installed within the grounds of Kyoto’s Kiyomizudera
description: They’re the first solar-powered, smart trash cans to be installed within the grounds of a temple or shrine anywhere in Japan. Recently, Japan has been in the midst of a refuse revolution in the way that it collects and transports trash. As a country with very few public trash cans that’s also experiencing waves of […]
content:
They’re the first solar-powered, smart trash cans to be installed within the grounds of a temple or shrine anywhere in Japan.

Recently, Japan has been in the midst of a refuse revolution in the way that it collects and transports trash. As a country with very few public trash cans that’s also experiencing waves of overtourism in many cities, there’s no time to waste in tackling the problem of what to do with the very real and very over-capacity volume of waste in many urban areas.

One of the most promising solutions is a series of solar-powered, smart trash cans called “SmaGO” by Japanese company Forcetec that have hit the scene in 80 different locations around the country as of this writing. Research shows that they’ve already been making an impact by reducing the frequency of trash collection times by about 70 percent in Tokyo’s Omotesando/Harajuku shopping district and by reducing litter–apart from cigarette butts–by 90 percent in Osaka’s Dotonburi canal area. Now, they’re also found in 19 areas of Japan’s ancient capital of Kyoto City–and in a first for the whole country, directly within the actual grounds of a temple or shrine.

Actually, UNESCO World Heritage Site Kiyomizudera, a temple of the Shingon Sect of Buddhism, was constructed before the capital even moved to modern-day Kyoto in 794 CE. It’s probably not the first place you’d think of to host a futuristic-sounding receptacle, but a line of SmaGO trash cans is now gracing its grounds inside of the Niomon Gate.

Kiyomizudera easily makes it into the top three most popular attractions for most visitors to Kyoto with its wide balcony offering sweeping views of the surrounding scenery year-round. During peak foliage season in the fall, it can even see up to 20,000-30,000 visitors per day. Up until now, the temple was struggling to accommodate the sheer volume of trash deposited in its bins despite sanitation workers emptying them around four times per day. The situation was dire enough that the religious corporation behind the temple gladly partnered with Forcetec to install the new bins, which have a function to automatically compress the accumulated trash to about one-fifth of its original volume. Workers are able to remotely check the status via a cloud network to optimize the time of removal, which is slated to be reduced to only once per day.

The SmaGO trash cans are also designed to promote recycling for glass bottles, cans, and plastic bottles and to make Japan’s somewhat complicated trash-sorting rules more visible. Color-coded labels with pictures and text in both Japanese and English on the cans should reduce barriers for foreign visitors as well.

Furthermore, one of the new receptacles is specifically intended for leftover beverages. A mechanism inside it separates bottles from the liquid and funnels the latter directly into a sewage pipe. As the shopping streets leading up to Kiyomizudera are packed with places to grab a quick bite to eat or drink while walking, this new one should help visitors dispose of any unwanted refreshment while mitigating the odor and leakage.

Time will tell whether the SmartGo smart trash cans make more than just a literal dent in the trash in Japan’s heavily touristed areas, even within sacred grounds. With several groups of them installed in Tokyo’s Akihabara electronics district just one week ago, it looks like the future is (not) full of wasted potential after all.

title: Complaints of bar scams from foreign tourists in Tokyo’s Shinjuku triple compared to last year
description: Japan’s tourism landscape keeps changing, but Kabukicho stays the same. Once upon a time, there were plans to build a kabuki theater in Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward, and this caused a section of it to be preemptively named Kabukicho, meaning, more or less, “Kabuki town.” The name stuck, but construction of the theater was later cancelled, […]
content:
Japan’s tourism landscape keeps changing, but Kabukicho stays the same.

Once upon a time, there were plans to build a kabuki theater in Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward, and this caused a section of it to be preemptively named Kabukicho, meaning, more or less, “Kabuki town.” The name stuck, but construction of the theater was later cancelled, and instead Kabukicho (pictured above) became one of the densest concentrations of bars, pubs, and host/hostess clubs in Japan.

Whether that outcome is something to be lamented or celebrated depends on the relative values one personally assigns to classical stage arts, liquid refreshment, and compensated companionship. I think we can pretty much all agree, though, that it’s unfortunate that Kabukicho has also become a major source of complaints about bars running scams to rip off customers, and it appears that the number of foreign tourists getting caught in such schemes has been rapidly rising.

Between January and October of this year, the Tokyo Metropolitan Police’s Shinjuku Precinct, whose jurisdiction includes Kabukicho, has received approximately 240 complaints from foreign tourists about being ripped off at bars located within the ward. This is roughly three times the number of complaints received for the same period in 2025.

A common pattern in the complaints is tourists being approached on the street by a barker, called a kyakuhiki/“customer puller” in Japanese. The barker will then lead the tourists to the bar, and when the bill is being settled at the end of the evening, the bar adds on additional charges without the customers’ knowledge or consent. Other textbook scams that ripoff bars have been known to run include exorbitant prices for otoshi (a small appetizer served upon seating at Japanese pubs) and tacking on shady, vaguely defined service or seating charges. In the case of host/hostess clubs, where the customer is required to pay both for their own food and drink as well as their companion’s, unscrupulous establishments may sneak extra orders and services onto the bill and say they were at the request of the host/hostess, even if the customer did not agree to them.

In total, the Shinjuku Precinct has received around 340 complaints of bar ripoffs within the ward so far this year, with the claimed damages coming to a total of roughly 390 million yen (US$2.45 million). That’s nearly triple the amount for the entire year of 2025, 140 million yen.

In looking through the complaints, the Tokyo Metropolitan Police say they’ve noticed a pattern of African kyakuhiki specifically targeting foreign tourists, whose lack of familiarity with Japanese bar industry standard practices might make them easier to trick. As part of a crackdown, on November 11 the police arrested a 62-year-old Nigerian resident of Japan on charges of running an unlicensed bar in Kabukicho.

With roughly 70 percent of the complaints regarding ripoff bars coming from foreign tourists, it’s difficult to say whether such scams as a whole are becoming more common, or if Japan’s ongoing inbound foreign tourism boom simply means that there are more potential victims who are more likely to go to the police with grievances. Kabukicho being filled with ripoff bars has long been common knowledge among Japanese natives and the country’s expat population, and with some of the schemes they pull being dishonest but not technically illegal, there’s a certain amount of embarrassment involved in admitting that you got tricked, likely in part due to lowered defenses because you were some combination of drunk and horny.

So what can you do to protect yourself? For starters, it’s best to exercise caution with kyakuhiki. Because of their association with ripoff joints, it’s become uncommon for businesses that are on the up and up to dispatch them much farther than maybe the front entrance of their establishment. The longer the march a kyakuhiki takes you on, the more likely it is that something fishy is going to happen, since that distance and disorientation (i.e. isolation and confusion) is often part of the setup. Geeting upfront information about service charges is also advisable if you’re not used to Japan’s bar scene, and the following phrases are good to know.

● Otoshi dai wa ikura desu ka? / How much does the otoshi cost?
● Teburu chaji wa arimasu ka? / Is there a table charge?
● Sekiryo wa arimasu ka? / Is there a seating charge?
● Sabisu chaji wa arimasu ka? / Is there a service charge?

If you want to be extra cautious, sticking to established chain pubs and bars is also an effective way to avoid scams. That’s not to say scams are common among independent establishments, but the large chains’ need to comply with all laws and regulations in order to not bring down their entire business group means that they can pretty much always be trusted not to rip you off.

And finally, don’t forget that it’s not just official kyakuhiki who try to lure victims into ripoff schemes, so should you meet an attractive stranger who seems unusually fixated on having a drink with you at a particular but unremarkable bar, that’s also probably a sign that bad things are afoot.

content:
Once again coming to fans around the world, except in Japan.

Uniqlo is no stranger to collaborations with Japan’s most beloved anime and manga franchises, so it seems only natural that they periodically team up with Studio Ghibli. The two have recently revealed that they’re ready for a brand-new batch of Ghibli UT Graphic T-shirts, with veteran anime film producer Toshio Suzuki even personally creating one of the featured illustrations.

Uniqlo describes this latest chapter of their partnership with:

The theme of the collection is “LIVE FOR TODAY, MY DEAR.” The UT designs feature iconic Studio Ghibli works, including photos taken by Thai artist Kanyada at the Ghibli Museum, Mitaka, new illustrations, and poster art used in exhibitions. The collection expresses the joy of cherishing each day and the rich worlds of Studio Ghibli’s works.

The collection consists of five adult-size T-shirts, and the one that fans’ eyes are probably going to immediately lock on to is this one, with the theme printed on the chest and a whole bunch of Ghibli characters flying and frolicking on the back.

Suzuki, who drew this illustration himself, says that the somewhat bewildered-looking pig standing next to Spirited Away’s No Name is meant to be his portrait of fellow Studio Ghibli co-founder Hayao Miyazaki, who often depicts himself as a pig in doodles.

▼ Suzuki also says he rushed through the drawing of little witch Kiki, but isn’t entirely unsatisfied with how it turned out.

Though you can find passionate fans of almost any Ghibli work, Totoro remains the most immediately recognizable symbol of the studio, so next we have a My Neighbor Totoro tee, with several different versions of the forest spirit lounging about, and even an appearance by the Catbus.

▼ Front

▼ Back

Howl’s Moving Castle is the inspiration for the last of the double-sided designs, with Calcifer and deceptively important Turnip Head on the front…

…and Heen sleepily, but doggedly, watching your back.

Switching over to the shirts that only feature artwork on the front, they still have plenty of illustrative impact, with a slew of Soot Sprites reminding us of places “where a world of mystery still lives on”…

…and Castle in the Sky/Laputa’s Robot Soldier making sure no one forgets which Ghibli film it hails from.

There are also four kids-size shirts, two of which are alternate versions of the Suzuki-illustrated Ghibli cast group shot and My Neighbor Totoro, and the other two being unique Howl’s Moving Castle and Spirited Away designs.

In what’s become a puzzling pattern, though, once again the Ghibli Uniqlo collection will be available internationally, but not in Japan. It’s not clear why Japan is always excluded from the collaboration, but that’s been the case for years now, and doesn’t seem likely to change anytime soon.

Prices and release dates vary by region, with Uniqlo stores and online shops operating in Malaysia, Thailand, and Taiwan offering them from December 14. European Uniqlo shops, including those in the U.K. and Spain, will have theirs on January 21, and Uniqlo U.S.A. has them listed as “arriving late January.”

title: Nara deer send record number of people to hospital, over 70 percent of patients are foreigners
description: Just because Nara’s deer are usually cute and calm doesn’t mean they’re not still wild animals who will mess you up if you give them a reason to. For anyone with the city of Nara on their Japan travel itinerary, Nara Park, with its herds of deer that roam freely across its grounds, is a […]
content:
Just because Nara’s deer are usually cute and calm doesn’t mean they’re not still wild animals who will mess you up if you give them a reason to.

For anyone with the city of Nara on their Japan travel itinerary, Nara Park, with its herds of deer that roam freely across its grounds, is a must-visit. Unfortunately, for some tourists the hospital has become a must-visit in Nara too, as this year has seen a record-setting number of people taken by ambulance to Nara Municipal Hospital for treatment for deer-induced injuries, with the majority being foreign visitors.

To recap, Nara’s deer are considered messengers of the gods under Shinto belief, and so they’re given more or less free reign to go wherever they want within the park. They’ve become very accustomed to human visitors and don’t scatter when people come near, and posing for pictures with the animals and feeding them some special deer cracker snacks purchased from venders in and around the park have become the top tourist activities in the town.

However, it’s important to remember that Nara’s deer are not domesticated. Despite their comparative comfort mingling with humans, they are still wild animals, and injuries can occur if proper caution isn’t exercised when interacting with them. In addition to biting and butting, the deers’ antlers can be incredibly sharp, with a near knife-like keenness to them, experts warn. They can become particularly aggressive around people who are carrying deer crackers, sometimes even following them throughout the park if they know the person hasn’t yet handed out the entire pack of treats.

▼ An elderly woman can be seen in this video describing how deer have nipped at her coat pockets if they think she still has deer crackers on her.

▼ The man seen at the start of this video also talks about having been bit on the leg by a Nara deer.

As of November 5, Nara Municipal Hospital reports having received 51 patients who were transported by ambulance to the facility for treatment for deer-induced injuries. This tops last year’s 46 patients and 2024’s 45, both of which were themselves records, which were themselves proportionally huge increases from previous years. Out of the 51 patients so far this year, over 70 percent have been foreigners.

● Patients taken by ambulance to Nara Municipal Hospital for deer-induced injuries
2026 (through November 5): 51
2025: 46
2024: 45
2023: 23
2022: 11
2021: 7
2020: 10
2019: 24
2018: 15
2017: 15

As for what’s causing the increase in injuries, the Nara administration is citing increases in both the number of visitors to Nara Park as well as the number of deer living within it.

It’s worth noting that the ratio of injuries to visitors hasn’t gone up, at least not compared to five years ago. In 2021, when Japan still had several international tourism-limiting pandemic protocols in place, Nara Park received around 46,000 foreign visitors. In 2025, that number grew to more than 3.5 million, so the percentage of visitors injured by deer has certainly decreased.

That said, such statistics will be of little comfort to anyone who does need to be taken to the hospital after an unfortunate altercation with a deer, and the Nara Deer Preservation Society cautions against getting too close to or petting deer that don’t seem receptive to such advances. They also warn against teasing deer by holding out crackers as if they’re being offered, then pulling them back without actually giving them to the animals. Finally, autumn is a time of year when visitors should be especially cautious, they add, as it’s mating season, when males can become particularly aggressive and territorial, so it’s advisable to give them extra space, especially if you see two male deer who are beefing with each other.

title: Are the viral fries at De Frites Staan Harajuku really worth the hype?
description: We find out what a local Japanese woman thinks of the Belgian fries obsession in Tokyo. Our reporter Natsuki Gojo prides herself on her willpower, as she has the strength to say no to a lot of things. One of the few things she can’t say no to, however, is potato chips, and she likes […]
content:
We find out what a local Japanese woman thinks of the Belgian fries obsession in Tokyo.

Our reporter Natsuki Gojo prides herself on her willpower, as she has the strength to say no to a lot of things. One of the few things she can’t say no to, however, is potato chips, and she likes them so much that sometimes she gets an overwhelming craving for them.

It was only a matter of time before the algorithm caught on to Natsuki’s weak spot, so her feed recently became flooded with chip recommendations, and one that caught her eye was a post that sang the praises of the fries at De Frites Staan Harajuku. This specialty shop serves frites, the style of French fries popular in Belgium and France, which are thick-cut and served in a cone, and they looked so good that she knew right away that she had to go and try them.

According to the store’s official Instagram account, dine-in customers can’t order fries on their own, so if you want to try just the fries, you’ll need to order takeout, and if you’re an early bird like Natsuki, it’s good to note that takeout orders start 30 minutes after the store opens.

Since she wanted to focus entirely on enjoying the frites, she decided to go with takeout, and from the two sizes available – small and regular – she ordered the small size for 1,188 yen (US$7.90).

There are both free and paid dipping sauces available, and Natsuki decided to try the popular Mayonnaise & Truffle sauce, which costs an additional 270 yen. After a short wait outside the store, Natsuki’s number was called and she was handed the most stylish-looking fries she’d ever seen. Both the sauce and the potatoes were presented beautifully, sitting nicely in the bright red cone as if they were just waiting for their close-up.

Impressed by their beauty, Natsuki was now keen to see if they tasted as good as they looked. First, she decided to try the fries on their own, without any of the dipping sauce.

Freshly fried and piping hot, these fries were like nothing she’d ever tasted before. Not only did they have an incredibly crispy exterior and a wonderfully light texture but the inside remained surprisingly fluffy and soft. She could also taste the lovely aroma of the potato skins, which were more than just a supporting act – they were the star of the show.

Next, she dipped the chips into the Mayonnaise & Truffle sauce, and they were just as delicious.

The rich creaminess of the mayonnaise paired beautifully with the potatoes, while the mushroom-like aroma of the truffle added a lovely extra dimension that made the combination seriously moreish. At this point, she was so enraptured by the frites that she didn’t want the experience to end, but at the same time, she wanted to eat them all while they were still piping hot. It was a wonderfully delicious dilemma.

The only drawback to the frites was how messy her hands got when eating them with the dipping sauce. There was so much sauce that, as she worked her way through them, she simply resigned herself to having saucy fingers, as they were too delicious for her to stop eating them.

There were paper napkins at the counter, but if you’re getting takeaway, Natsuki recommends bringing a small pack of wet wipes with you so you can fully enjoy the experience.

It’s now been several days since she tried the frites, and Natsuki still can’t get the memory of the wonderfully crispy-outside, fluffy-inside texture out of her mind. Even her friend who went along with her has been messaging her to ask when they can go for another visit, so it’s safe to say that these viral frites really are worth the hype.

So next time you’re exploring the tight alleyways and bright storefronts of Harajuku, be sure to stop and refuel at De Frites Staan…but be aware that you might wind up dreaming about their deliciousness for days afterwards.

title: Akihabara restaurant with 1.7 million sushi bowl options will have us coming back again and again
description: A virtually inexhaustible addition to our to-eat backlog was hiding on the quiet side of Akihabara Station. Variety is the name of the game in Akihabara. Tokyo’s anime/video game district offers an amazing selection of both new releases and classic titles and merch waiting to be discovered by discerning fans in second-hand shops, allowing you […]
content:
A virtually inexhaustible addition to our to-eat backlog was hiding on the quiet side of Akihabara Station.

Variety is the name of the game in Akihabara. Tokyo’s anime/video game district offers an amazing selection of both new releases and classic titles and merch waiting to be discovered by discerning fans in second-hand shops, allowing you to find the exact mix of things that appeal to you.

And there’s a similar situation going on at a sushi bowl restaurant in Akihabara, one that we didn’t know about until a recent walk through the neighborhood.

Uodon, whose name literally translates as “Fish Bowl,” opened in 2025, but its location means that a lot of visitors to Akihabara might not have noticed it. It’s only about two blocks from Akihabara Station, but it’s to the east of the station, whereas most of the tourist-attracting stores and arcades are on the west side.

Like a lot of restaurants in Japan, Uodon has a signboard out front showing some of its menu items. Unlike most restaurants, though, Uodon’s board has about 150 different options on it.

And yes, this still only counts as “some” of what you can order. By picking and choosing your own sushi rice bowl toppings, you can actually make more than 1.7 million different combinations, the restaurant says.

While some people might revel in this sort of fish-selecting freedom. Uodon does also recognize that having so many choices could also have a paralyzing effect on some people, hence the 150 suggestions on the board. The restaurant also lists the top three most popular orders among male and female customers, and our Japanese-language reporter P.K. Sanjun decided to take their advice and order the most popular bowl for guys, the Seared Salmon Belly with Mayo and Hidden Negitoro, for 930 yen (US$5.85).

Mayonnaise, as you’re probably already aware, isn’t a conventional condiment for sushi, but P.K. could see why it’s popular with this restaurant’s clientele. Diners in Akihabara tend to gravitate more towards “grub” than “cuisine,” and restaurants with filling, strongly flavored dishes tend to do well here. So while this is definitely a break with tradition, he was willing to give it a chance.

Placed before him, the Seared Salmon Belly with Mayo and Hidden Negitoro Bowl certainly looked the part of a sushi bowl given a junk food remix. With the glistening mayo dotted with a generous shake of black pepper, he braced himself for the possibility of all those seasonings being employed to mask the unpleasantness of some sub-par fish…

…but, thankfully, this turned out to not be the case at all! While Uodon does have non-traditional menu items like this, they also have classics of vinegared rice and fish without any unusual innovative flourishes, so the fish has to be good enough to stand on its own merits. The salmon in P.K.’s bowl was actually quite good, just given an extra impactful punch with the contributions of the mayo and pepper.

As he dug deeper into the vinegared sushi rice, he came to the negitoro, minced fatty tuna with green onion, buried under the top layer of grains. P.K. felt that the negitoro was on the greasy side, though it’s hard for us to say how much of that might be from mayo dripping down into it, but the tuna’s delicious flavor was still intact.

Fully satisfied, P.K. soon came back to Uodon to try something still creative but a little less outlandish, a marinated chirashi (mixed sashimi) bowl with avocado, which was excellent too.

P.K. later learned that Uodon is actually a chain, though they only have about 50 locations nationwide, and most branches tend to be farther outside the city center than Akihabara. Because of that, it might take a little extra walking to get to one, but the quality of their food has won P.K.’s heart and stomach, and with so many options to choose from, he’s going to be able to make a whole lot of return trips until he runs out of things to try.

title: Cup Noodles go isekai in crossovers with three of Japan’s other favorite foods [Taste test]
description: Three ways to send your taste buds on an isekai journey, no collision with Truck-kun required. The isekai/alternate world genre of anime/manga often starts from traumatic events. Getting hit by a truck, stabbed by a maniac, or some other sudden life-ending set of circumstances is usually what the protagonist has to go through before they […]
content:
Three ways to send your taste buds on an isekai journey, no collision with Truck-kun required.

The isekai/alternate world genre of anime/manga often starts from traumatic events. Getting hit by a truck, stabbed by a maniac, or some other sudden life-ending set of circumstances is usually what the protagonist has to go through before they can be reborn in a new life and environment so that they can set out on new adventures.

Thankfully, Cup Noodle’s isekai experience doesn’t have any such unpleasantries as a prerequisite. Instead, all you’ve got to do is walk into a Japanese supermarket or convenience store and grab a cup of the new Cup Noodle Isekai Gattai series, which fuses maker Nissin’s flagship instant ramen with one of three other much-loved food icons in Japan. We’d been looking forward to them since their announcement last month, and with all three isekai Cup Noodles having gone on sale on November 9, today we finally get to try them.

The three crossover contributors here are Gindaco, east Japan’s favorite chain of takoyaki (octopus dumpling) shops, Karamucho, the country’s most popular brand of spicy potato crisp snacks, and Gohan Desu Yo, a brand of simmered seaweed paste that’s usually spread over white rice.

Each isekai Cup Noodle is easy to make. Just add hot water, let the noodles cook for three minutes, then pour in the additional ingredient packet and give everything a quick stir before you dig in.

For this article, taste-testing duties were performed by our Japanese-language reporter Yayoi Saginomiya. Yayoi was looking for two things here: how well the isekai Cup Noodles recreated the flavor of their respective guest stars, and also how good the resulting combination tasted. For each, she’ll be grading them on a scale of one to five stars.

● Seafood Cup Noodle Gohan Desu Yo

Our first alternate world brings together the Seafood flavor of Cup Noodle with Gohan Desu Yo. Combining seafood with seaweed seems like an easy path to scrumptious success, but it turns out things aren’t quite that simple.

Once you add the Gohan Desu Yo paste into the broth, it quickly melts away, losing its texture and much of its flavor too. At the same time, the standard Seafood Cup Noodle broth ends up feeling sort of diluted too. This is probably a result of merging two flavors that have similarities, but which are still different enough that they don’t really enhance each other, making the combination feel a little lacking in direction. It doesn’t taste bad, but if you like either Seafood Cup Noodle or Gohan Desu Yo, you’ll probably enjoy them both better eaten on their own.

Recreation of Gohan Desu Yo: ★★☆☆☆
Overall deliciousness: ★★☆☆☆

● Cup Noodle Gindaco

This isekai combo uses the standard Cup Noodle flavor and its soy sauce-based broth. Add in the Gindaco oil packet, though, and the broth’s flavor becomes almost exactly the same as Gindaco’s takoyaki sauce, which is sort of like a sweet Worcester. The seaweed flakes, another takoyaki topping, really make their presence felt in the aroma that rises from the cup, and the “octopus-style balls” very much do remind us of the center of a takoyaki.

What with this being essentially a noodle soup, though, you don’t really get Gindaco’s touch of crispness that it cooks into the surface of its takoyaki breading, but the Gindaco Cup Noodles really will remind fans of the dumplings’ flavor, and makes for a fine choice even if you aren’t aware of the tie-in.

Recreation of Gindaco: ★★★☆☆
Overall deliciousness: ★★★☆☆

● Cup Noodle Karamucho

Now this was amazing! We start with Curry Cup Noodle. Which, to Yayoi’s tongue, has a touch of sweetness to it. Then we add in Karamucho hot chili powder, which adds a sharply stimulating heat and garlic notes too.

The resulting flavor is so good that it completely justifies the extremely unorthodox ramen topping of potato. Yes, this isekai Cup Noodle includes what are basically little flattened-out tater tots, and when they’re soaked in such flavorful spiciness, they taste fantastic.

Recreation of Karamucho: ★★★★☆
Overall deliciousness: ★★★★★

So in the end, sort of like within the isekai anime genre itself, we found a lot of difference in quality from one isekai Cup Noodle to another. That said, one person’s parallel-world paradise could be another’s alternate-dimension abyss of despair, and reactions to these unusual noodles is going to depend heavily on personal preferences, so we recommend giving any that catch your interest a try during the limited time they’ll be available for.

title: Ichiran Japan is giving away free 2027 desk calendars, and here’s how to get them
description: The perfect gift for the ramen lover in your life. If you’ve ever been on the hunt for a unique ramen experience in Japan, you may have come across a chain called Ichiran. Known for its thin, straight noodles and hearty tonkotsu pork bone broth, what makes the chain particularly unique is its partitioned counter […]
content:
The perfect gift for the ramen lover in your life.

If you’ve ever been on the hunt for a unique ramen experience in Japan, you may have come across a chain called Ichiran. Known for its thin, straight noodles and hearty tonkotsu pork bone broth, what makes the chain particularly unique is its partitioned counter seating, known as the “Taste Concentration Counter”, which allows you to focus entirely on the noodles that are served to you through a bamboo screen.

▼  The “Taste Concentration Counter”

This private booth-style ramen experience is one that’s particularly loved by international visitors, as you submit your order on paper and food is served through the bamboo screen so you don’t ever have to speak with staff. While you can take a memento of the trip home with you in the form of dried noodle packs, the counter seating is something you usually have to leave behind. That’s all changing for a limited time, though, as the chain is giving away desk calendars that look like a miniature counter seat, allowing you to enjoy the Ichiran experience every day of the year.

▼ The miniature booth comes as a DIY kit, which is said to be easy to assemble.

This year’s edition has an extra special feature, as it includes a miniature bowl of the chain’s famous Hakata Thin Straight Noodles, to mark the 10th anniversary of the noodles. The calendar also comes in a special envelope modelled on Ichiran’s ramen order sheet, so gift-givers can circle their preferred options and write a message on it before adding a stamp and posting it through the mail.


The 2027 calendars won’t be available for sale, but they will be available through two distribution channels, with different start dates and eligibility requirements. Customers who place an order at the chain’s online store  from 11 a.m. on 16 November, with a total of at least 1,000 yen (US$6.50) excluding shipping fees, can indicate whether they would like a calendar included during checkout.

For those visiting a restaurant, the giveaway begins at 10 a.m. on 1 December at branches across Japan. Customers can receive a calendar by ordering one bowl of ramen or purchasing an Ichiran souvenir product. However, this offer is limited to members of the Ichiran official app, so customers who haven’t registered yet will need to sign up before claiming their gift. Simply show the membership screen to a staff member when ordering.

As the calendars are being made in limited quantities and only available while stocks last, you’ll want to get in early to make sure you get your hands on them. Because, as we learned with Ichiran’s recent at-home countertop release, these things tend to disappear early.

title: Yesterday’s cooking oil powers 410,000 pink winter sakura lights along Tokyo’s Meguro River
description: Who says you have to wait until spring for cherry blossoms? A wide river coated in pink petals, adorned on either side by rows of stunningly gorgeous cherry blossom trees amid a sprawling cityscape, the Meguro River in spring is one of Tokyo’s must-see sakura viewing spots. Running through the neighborhoods of Gotanda and Osaki, […]
content:
Who says you have to wait until spring for cherry blossoms?

A wide river coated in pink petals, adorned on either side by rows of stunningly gorgeous cherry blossom trees amid a sprawling cityscape, the Meguro River in spring is one of Tokyo’s must-see sakura viewing spots. Running through the neighborhoods of Gotanda and Osaki, this two-kilometer (1.2-mile) stretch of sakura trees creates of massive pink canopy for visitors to enjoy, and most Tokyo guidebooks will feature a photo of this iconic spot.

Although not every trip to Tokyo coincides with the blossoms, landing a few months earlier in December or January means you don’t necessarily have to miss out on appreciating this pink scenery—it’ll just be LEDs instead of actual petals.

▼ That’s not to say there aren’t different cherry blossom varieties at other times of the year, like around November at Senmi Shikizakura no Sato in Aichi.

Every winter, the Meguro area hosts the Meguro River Minna no Illumination, turning the once bare cherry branches along the river into a glowing pink ‘winter sakura’ display. Running from December 4 to January 31, between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., around 410,000 pink lights will be stretched across the riverbanks, creating a sensory clash as the warming sight of the pink trees battles with the cold of the winter air.

There are many people who eschew winter illuminations due to its environmental impact, but this light display operates on a 100-percent self-generated, closed-loop energy system powered by recycled biodiesel. Local restaurants, businesses, and neighborhood households collect their used cooking oil throughout the year, which gets refined to power the generators, meaning that the oil that may have been used to cook your dinner the previous night might be contributing to tonight’s stroll along the river.

▼ Gotanda Station (五反田駅) is the uppermost landmark on the map, with the yellow Gotanda Waterfront Plaza (五反田ふれあい水辺広場) marked just below it, and the stretch of sakura trees running down to the southeast past Osaki Station (大崎駅).

Along with the lights, the area around Gotanda Waterfront Plaza (a three-minute walk from Gotanda Station) will also feature an interactive light-ripple art installation by creative unit Zero by Zero, which is also powered by the same biodiesel (tentatively available until December 31), and community recycling pop-ups.

A small opening-day ceremony with local school bands and riverboats will be held at 4:00 p.m. on December 4, but between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. a hands-on workshop to make your own kaleidoscope using waste materials such as cardboard and paper tubes will allow you discover new charms in familiar scenery.

If you’re out exploring the area over the holidays, taking a brisk walk under a couple hundred thousand glowing pink lights is a great way to experience the joy of spring a couple of months early.

title: Life-size Gundam head going on display in Osaka, hopefully will find permanent home
description: Gundam head arrives in Osaka ahead of Gundam Base. Osaka has been making a big push recently to obtain official status as Japan’s backup capital should a major disaster knock out government facilities in Tokyo. Its case rests largely on compliance with criteria related to population, economic importance, and geography, but soon Osaka will be […]
content:
Gundam head arrives in Osaka ahead of Gundam Base.

Osaka has been making a big push recently to obtain official status as Japan’s backup capital should a major disaster knock out government facilities in Tokyo. Its case rests largely on compliance with criteria related to population, economic importance, and geography, but soon Osaka will be able to boast yet another fine feature: the full-size head of Gundam on display within the city.

The head unit of the iconic anime mecha was first seen in Yokohama, where it sat on the shoulders of the life-size RX-78F00 Gundam at the Gundam Factory Yokohama. The 18-meter (59-foot) tall statue was removed in the spring of 2024 and relocated to Osaka for the Expo 2025 world’s fair, serving as the centerpiece of the Gundam Next Future Pavilion. With the Expo finished, the RX-78F00/E (as the updated Osaka version of the statue was called) has been dismantled, but the head will be going on display at the new Lucua South entertainment complex in Osaka’s Umeda neighborhood next month.

▼ The head, which will be displayed on the building’s 10th floor, stands 2.2 meters tall and weighs approximately 370 kilograms (815.7 pounds), so there’s little chance of anyone running off with it.

The head is just one part of a planned proliferation of Gundam fun coming to Lucua South. Scheduled to open in February of next year is a brand-new Gundam Base Osaka specialty shop, filled with Gunpla plastic model kits and other merch. As a touch of local flavor, Gundam’s spherical mascot robot Haro will get a makeover to make him look like a takoyaki octopus dumpling, Osaka’s representative street food snack.

▼ The takoyaki Haro will talk too, but there’s no word yet on whether or not he’ll speak in the distinctive Osaka dialect of Japanese.

Anime fan shoppers won’t have to wait all the way until February, though, as high-end figure brand Tamashii Nations will also be opening a new branch in Lucua South on December 2, with statues of the original Gundam and Dragon Ball’s Goku greeting visitors.

▼ A figure of the RX-78F00/E, in the pose it struck during the Expo, will be on offer.

Two days later, on December 4, an official Gundam Card Game store will also open inside the building…

…and fashionable fans of anime mecha can get their fix the soonest of all, with a Strict-G store, stocked with items from the Gundam apparel/accessory line of the same name, opening in Lucua South on November 24.

▼ Two new Osaka Gundam Yokosuka jackets will be available, one with an image of Osaka Castle, the other with the city’s name written in kanji characters.

Getting back to the Gundam head, though the display starts on December 4, there’s currently no announced end date. Common sense would suggest that it’ll be on display at least until the Gundam Base Osaka opens in February, and it’s hard to imagine a better place for it to remain after that than in the store itself, but still, checking it out sooner rather than later is probably the smart move.

title: Tokyo police arrest the Ame-zing Spider-Man
description: Your unfriendly rainy-day Spider-Man. For nearly a decade, Tokyo had been terrorized by a wall-crawling bandit who would climb into the higher floors of buildings and make off with whatever cash or valuables he could get his sticky fingers on. His name was Yuki Horiguchi, but to police, he’s known as the Ame-zing Spider-Man. That’s […]
content:
Your unfriendly rainy-day Spider-Man.

For nearly a decade, Tokyo had been terrorized by a wall-crawling bandit who would climb into the higher floors of buildings and make off with whatever cash or valuables he could get his sticky fingers on. His name was Yuki Horiguchi, but to police, he’s known as the Ame-zing Spider-Man.

That’s not a typo in his nickname. The Japanese word for “rain” is “ame” (ah-may), and this Spider-Man’s MO was to strike on rainy days in particular. Likely relying on the fact that people tend to not look up when it’s raining, Horiguchi would access the roofs of buildings using emergency stairs on the outside, and then rappel down to a window, breaking through it to access the building and burglarize it.

This is what he did on one rainy day in December 2025. Climbing down a rope and gaining entry to the sixth-floor balcony of a head spa in Taito, he stole a portable safe and a wallet before moving to an adjacent building and stealing about 110,000 yen (US$690) in cash.

It isn’t clear how police managed to catch the Ame-zing Spider-Man this time, but the thing about getting a cool nickname from the police is that they know exactly when it’s you who committed a crime. Horiguchi had already been picked up by law enforcement in 2019 for similar burglaries on rainy days, so it isn’t taking much to link this and some 50 other incidents in the Greater Tokyo Area over the past year alone to Spidey.

Many readers of the news online took serious issue with a criminal being given the honorable name of “Spider-Man.”

“He should apologize to the real Spider-Man!”
“Normally, I’d say talented criminals should put their skills toward doing good work, but this guy kind of seems really cut out to be a burglar more than anything.”
“Giving him a name like that shows a complete lack of sincerity towards the victims.”
“He doesn’t deserve the name Spider-Man.”
“50 times?! They can’t let that slide.”
“That’s lame.”
“The cop who came up with ‘Ame-zing Spider-Man’ should be arrested too.”
“I wonder if Sony will complain about this.”
“Seems like a lot of effort and risk for 110,000 yen.”
“More like Lupin III than Spider-Man.”
“He doesn’t have any mutant powers. He’s just a bad Daredevil.”

It seems rather likely that this repeat offender will be spending a lot of time behind bars. Perhaps he can learn there that with a great nickname comes great attention from the police, and finally knock it off with this life of crime.

title: Ichiran releases an at-home counter kit that turns your desk into a ramen restaurant
description: Iconic ramen chain brings out an exclusive product so you can fully focus on the taste of the noodles. Amongst all the many ramen restaurants in Japan, Ichiran stands out for its unique dining experience, where customers sit at a long counter with private partitions and receive their noodles through a bamboo screen. The unusual […]
content:
Iconic ramen chain brings out an exclusive product so you can fully focus on the taste of the noodles.

Amongst all the many ramen restaurants in Japan, Ichiran stands out for its unique dining experience, where customers sit at a long counter with private partitions and receive their noodles through a bamboo screen. The unusual seating layout is what the chain calls its “Aji Shuuchuu Counter”, or “Taste Concentration Counter”, as the private seating allows you to concentrate solely on the taste of the noodles, free from the gaze of others around you.

Now, the chain is giving us a way to enjoy the special dining setup at home, with the release of an exclusive “Taste Concentration Counter Kit”. We were fortunate enough to receive one in the office recently, so our reporter Ahiruneko got straight to trying it out, using the kit to turn his desk into an Ichiran restaurant.

The kit requires some assembly, so Ahiruneko started by inserting the side panels into the overhead sign and countertop pieces.

▼ Then he attached the reinforcement parts…

▼ …and finished by inserting the bamboo blind into the back of the setup.

▼ Now he was ready to eat!

The Taste Concentration Counter turned out to be tiny, but it displayed impressive attention to detail, with the front sign covered in explanatory text and the bamboo blind raising and lowering as it would at an actual restaurant.

▼ It even came with the side sign details, which includes instructions on how to place your order.

The most impressive thing, however, turned out to be the call button, because when you press it, you hear the same familiar chime played in Ichiran restaurants!

It was far more Ichiran-like than Ahiruneko had expected, allowing him to realise his dreams of opening a totally new branch of the chain in the office, which he dubbed the “Ichiran SoraNews24” branch.

▼ It may not be the most impressive branch, but it’s certainly a fun one.

Ahiruneko couldn’t help but smile upon opening his tiny branch, which consisted of one counter seat, set up neatly on his desk.

The only thing missing from the kit was a tiny chef to go with it, so Ahiruneko stepped in to take on noodle-cooking duties.

With everyone else in the office engrossed in their writing, Ahiruneko continued running the branch on his own, and when he lifted the bamboo screen, he felt a rush of excitement at what was to come.

▼ Ta daaaa! A hot bowl of Ichiran ramen!

Even though he was the one serving himself, Ahiruneko loved the setup, and was impressed at how the opening was just wide enough for the ramen bowl to fit perfectly.

Now he had the ideal ramen-eating setup on his desk, where he could concentrate entirely on the bowl in front of him…

▼ …without worrying about his boss and colleagues staring at him.

The Taste Concentration Counter was the perfect sanctuary where he could remain blissfully unaware of any potential side-eye from his higher-up colleague (上司) and company president (社長).

To really get into the Ichiran mood, you need to hunch over and slurp your noodles, so that’s exactly what Ahiruneko did.

By removing everything other than the counter from his field of vision, he was able to trick his brain into thinking he was actually at Ichiran.

Though he looked a bit like a student hiding a snack behind an upright textbook, the Flavour Concentration Counter Kit is enclosed by walls on three sides, so the chances of anyone noticing his noodle moment remained extremely low.

Even the workmate opposite him would never dream that he was having an Ichiran experience right there in the office.

▼ Hunched over a laptop? Or a bowl of noodles?

It didn’t take long for Ahiruneko to finish all his noodles, but as there was still some broth left, he did what any noodle lover should do at this point.

▼ He pressed the call button to order a noodle refill (known as “kaedama” in Japanese).

▼ Leaping up to attend to his own order, Ahiruneko headed over to the kitchen to boil up his kaedama.

▼ Then, back at his desk, the bamboo blind went up.


▼ And in came his extra serving of noodles!

▼ Ahiruneko, playing the role of both staff and customer with equal amounts of joy.

For Ahiruneko, a visit to Ichiran isn’t complete until you’ve ordered a noodle refill, so he was thrilled that he could recreate this ideal visit from the comfort of his office desk.

If you’re like Ahiruneko and absolutely love the unique feel of Ichiran’s Taste Concentration Counter, then he highly recommends purchasing this product while it’s available.

▼ This tiny model has a lot more finesse than the homemade cardboard setup we created in the past.

The kit, released to celebrate the 10th anniversary of its souvenir product, Ichiran Ramen Hakata Thin Straight Noodles, comes with either five servings of the noodles, for 3,850 yen (US$25.00), or 10 servings for 4,980 yen. Available while stocks last, the 10-serving set is only available at the online store, while the five-serving set can be purchased online and at physical stores right around the country.

How to create and customise your own bear for maximum cuteness.

Starbucks makes news every year for its hotly anticipated Christmas collection in Japan, and this year the star of the show is an incredibly cute tumbler called the Bearista Glass.

This exclusive new product looks adorable straight out of the box, with the chain’s Bearista character sitting cute with a star between its paws.

The red straw and Santa hat give the bear a festive look, but the real magic happens when you remove the lid to fill the glass with your favourite drink.

Though you could fill the bottle with water, the bear really comes to life when it’s filled with colourful drinks. And if you have trouble figuring out what type of drinks work well for the bear, Starbucks has some ideas to get you started.

As the tumblers can be used as soon as you purchase them, these drinks can be ordered with staff at the store, so you can enjoy your new bear from the get-go.

▼ The first suggestion is an iced Starbucks latte, which brings to life a light brown bear.

▼ Those wanting a brighter bear can opt for a Mango Passion Tea Frappuccino without cream

▼ Those wanting a more mellow hue can opt for the calming hues of an iced Matcha Tea Latte.

The options, though, are truly endless, with fruit teas giving you everything from berry red to dark crimson hues, and soft drinks giving you even more colours to play with.

▼ The chain also suggests matching your drink to the colour of your oshi, or object of your affections, as a display of fan support.

With each Bearista Glass priced at 4,600 yen (US$28.77), you can get your money’s worth by trying out drinks in all colours of the rainbow. Not only will you get to enjoy a variety of different flavours, you’ll also get to greet a lot of bears, before settling on your favourites.

title: Move aside, Asahi Super Dry – Asahi Spice Beer is in town, and it’s hotter than you think
description: Meet the surprisingly fiery beer that’s on everyone’s lips right now. When a lot of overseas people think about Japanese beer, Japan’s world-famous brand “Asahi Super Dry” might come to mind. However, right now, there’s a new type of Asahi making news in Japan, and rather than being dry, it’s surprisingly fiery, as the brew […]
content:
Meet the surprisingly fiery beer that’s on everyone’s lips right now.

When a lot of overseas people think about Japanese beer, Japan’s world-famous brand “Asahi Super Dry” might come to mind. However, right now, there’s a new type of Asahi making news in Japan, and rather than being dry, it’s surprisingly fiery, as the brew is made with jalapenos.

Called Asahi Spice Beer, you can find the new tipple at convenience stores, supermarkets, and liquor shops, the latter of which is where we found ours, being sold in 350-millilitre (12-ounce) cans for 195 yen, (US$1.22)…

▼ …and six-packs for 1,094 yen.

Released on 21 October, after being test-marketed in 2024, the beer is already proving to be popular, as we had to visit six stores to find it. It immediately caught our eye from the shelf, with its red-hot hue and fiery details, and the words “Brewed from quality beer ingredients and jalapeno pepper” under the golden name, “Asahi Spice Beer“.

After hearing from a friend that the beer didn’t have too much of a kick to it, we didn’t feel that we had anything to worry about with the heat levels in the drink. After all, how spicy can a beer be?

▼ With that thought in mind, we popped open the can.

Pouring some of it into a glass, it looked like an ordinary beer, and there wasn’t any noticeable spicy aroma.

▼ Feeling unsure of what to expect, we raised the glass and took a sip, only to find…

▼ … it was spicy!!

Though we’d only taken a tiny sip, the heat was unmistakable. This wasn’t a case of mild spiciness, as our friend had suggested, because within seconds, our tongue, lips and throat began to tingle.

It was a reaction that took us completely by surprise, and what was even more unexpected was the flavour, as it was utterly delicious. The first thing you taste is the crispness and umami you’d expect from a good beer, with just the right amount of bitterness, and then the heat from the jalapenos comes bolting in, lingering in the carbonation and leaving you with a sense of refreshment and spiciness at the same time.

Rather than getting in the way of things, the jalapenos actually added a nice accent in flavour. That said, there were moments when the heat lingered longer than expected, but after trying the beer with food, the heat took on another dimension.

Trying it with a bowl of oden, the spice beer became even more refreshing, with the heat bringing out the flavours of the simmered ingredients.

Usually, eating spicy food makes us want to drink more beer, but this time it was the other way around – drinking the beer made us want to eat more oden. Together, they worked a treat, and after dinner, the beer went well with a square of dark chocolate too.

After trying the beer, we were reminded that life really is better with a little spice. And the spice in this beer is nothing to sneeze at, as it’s a stimulating tipple that’ll enliven your entire palate with every sip.

In fact, once you’ve had one of these, you might find yourselves like us, hankering for another. The release is well-timed too, as it’s a surprisingly good winter warmer, so be sure to keep an eye out for it next time you’re browsing the aisles in Japan.

title: “Sweet sake” with yuzu is coming to Japan’s wonderful world of hot canned drinks this winter
description: Morinaga goes to Kochi in its search for a new spin on a traditional Japanese winter drink. Japan is a country that really gets into the spirit of each season, and not just in terms of fashions and festivals. As we get into the back half of autumn, more and more hot drinks start appearing […]
content:
Morinaga goes to Kochi in its search for a new spin on a traditional Japanese winter drink.

Japan is a country that really gets into the spirit of each season, and not just in terms of fashions and festivals. As we get into the back half of autumn, more and more hot drinks start appearing in convenience stores and vending machines. You can always count on hot coffee and green tea to always make an appearance, but each year also brings a selection of new entries into this warming, relaxing segment of the drink market, and one that we’ll be seeing soon is yuzu amazake.

Amazake literally translates as “sweet sake,” and yes, just like conventional sake, it’s a beverage made from fermented rice. Aside from that, though, amazake bears little resemblance to its more internationally famous rice wine cousin. For one thing, amazake is non-alcoholic. It’s also opaque and thicker in consistency, sort of a rice-based smoothie with a sweet flavor.

Though it can be drunk cold, amazake’s consistency makes it especially well-suited to heating up on a cold winter’s day so that it can warm you up from the inside. Japanese confectionery and beverage maker Morinaga has been selling canned amazake for many years, but they’ll be trying something new this winter with Kin no Kaoru Amazake Yuzu (“Golden Scent Amazake Yuzu”). The customary rich, sweet amazake flavor here gets an added twist with the introduction of a little touch of yuzu juice, sourced from Japan’s most prestigious producer of the sweetly sharp citrus fruit, Kochi Prefecture. The result, Morinaga says, is a fragrant, sweet, and soothing concoction that’s perfect for when you need to take a break and reward yourself as you’re crossing things off your to-do list ahead of the end-of-the-year holiday season.

Kin no Kaoru Amazake Yuzu goes on sale December 1.
